To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have measured the γ-ray spectrum in the energy range up to 90 MeV for the first time.
the energy spectra of γ rays from fission of 235U with neutrons of energy 0.5 MeV has been measured in the range of energies from 10 to 90 MeV.
we have measured the spectrum of γ-rays emitted in the fission of 235U induced by neutrons with an energy of 1.5 MeV.
In summary, our research is concerned with
γ rays in the energy range of 10–90 MeV, and the results are in good agreement with the existing experimental data and theoretical calculations.
the study of the energy spectra of γ rays from fission reactions in the high-energy region.
the study of the high-energy component of the γ-ray spectrum from the fission of 235U with neutrons of thermal energy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the probability of γ emission is very small, but not equal to zero in this energy range.
the probability of γ emission in the neutron-induced fisson reaction of 235 U nuclei decreases with increasing γ-ray energy.
, in the neutron-induced fissions of 235U and 238U, the γ-ray spectrum has a maximum in the energy region 10–20 MeV and a long tail in the energy region above 30 MeV.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the probability of the γ-ray emission in the energy range from 10 to 36 MeV increases from 0.2% to 1%.
the probability of γ emission is not more than 10% for energies above 36 MeV and is about 1.3% at the maximum energy of the fission fragment.
the spectrum of γ radiation in the energy range of 10–36 MeV has a pronounced maximum at an energy of about 30 MeV.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the yield of γ-ray emission is higher than the yield of charged-particle emission.
the energy dependence of γ-ray emission probability is not a monotonic function.
the spectrum of γ-ray emission from the 235U(n,f) reaction is not monotonically decreasing in the energy range of 10–90MeV.
